scenario.title: The camps at dawn
scenario.subtitle: Prentiss's and Sherman's camps, Fraley Field to Shiloh Church

objective.name: the camp line from Rhea Field to Spain Field

victory.attackerHolds: The Confederates hold the camp line at 09:30. (In 1862 Prentiss's camps were lost by about 09:00; Sherman held the church ridge until about 10:00.)
victory.defenderHolds: The camps are still in Union hands at 09:30. (In 1862 they were not: Prentiss's two brigades were swept from their camps by about 09:00.)

victory.draw: The camps are still contested at 09:30.

text: Before dawn on 6 April 1862 Col. Everett Peabody's patrol ran into Confederate pickets in Fraley Field, so the surprise Johnston and Beauregard had planned was lost before their main line stepped off.
The Confederacy went to war to preserve slavery; the army now coming through the woods was fighting for that cause.
Union warnings had been brushed aside the day before, so the camps were unentrenched and Prentiss's and Sherman's divisions, among the greenest in Grant's army, had to fight where they slept.

Hardee's line came on about 06:30 with brigades tangled together, many men carrying obsolete flintlocks and smoothbores, and struck Rhea Field in piecemeal attacks: a hard, even fight, not a story of Southern invincibility.
Hold the camps as long as you can: in 1862 Prentiss's brigades were swept away by about 09:00 and Sherman held the church ridge until about 10:00, buying time for the divisions behind.

scenario.positionsNote: Union formations start in or beside their camps at 05:00 (Sherman's report places Hildebrand east and Buckland west of Shiloh Meeting-House; the Handbook places Peabody's and Miller's camps north of Fraley, Seay and Spain fields). Hardee's line (Cleburne left, Wood centre, Shaver right, Gladden far right) starts south-west of the camps and steps off at 06:30 (Handbook and NPS plaque O; Daniel's map caption says 06:00). Bragg's and Polk's brigades enter at the times they came into action (Handbook, Daniel). All positions Inferred.
scenario.strengthNote: Union strengths are 5 April present-for-duty totals (Handbook App. A, from the OR revised abstract), not dawn effectives. Confederate strengths disagree between the Handbook, the NPS corps plaque and a rounded online compile; each formation carries its own method. Battery crews are a game value of 20 per gun.
scenario.historyNote: Peabody's patrol found Hardee's skirmishers about 04:55, but the Confederate line broke Peabody's and Miller's brigades by about 09:00 (Peabody was killed), and Sherman, wounded, held the Shiloh Church ridge until about 10:00 before falling back to the Hamburg-Purdy road.

outcome: Peabody's patrol met Hardee's skirmishers in Fraley Field about 04:55, so the Confederates never reached the camps unseen. Their main line, delayed until about 06:30, overlapped Prentiss's division and broke Peabody's brigade by about 08:45 (Peabody was killed) and Miller's by about 09:00, after Gladden fell mortally wounded at Spain Field and Chalmers extended the attack.

Prentiss's survivors fell back toward Pittsburg Landing, and some joined the line later called the Hornets' Nest. On the right, Hildebrand's and Buckland's brigades and Waterhouse's battery held Rhea Field against piecemeal attacks until about 09:30; Sherman, wounded, held the church ridge until about 10:00 before falling back to the Hamburg-Purdy road.

casualties.basis: No source gives losses for 05:00-09:30 alone. Over the whole battle Peabody's brigade lost 721 and Miller's 450 killed, wounded and missing (Staff Ride Handbook App. A). Inside this window the 6th Mississippi lost about 300 of 425 men in Rhea Field in under an hour (Daniel; NPS).

text: From about 10:00 W. H. L. Wallace's and Prentiss's men hold an old farm road on the east edge of Duncan Field, with Hurlbut's division at Sarah Bell's field and the Peach Orchard on their left.
The Confederates come on one or two brigades at a time: the Staff Ride Handbook counts eight uncoordinated attacks here between 10:30 and 15:30, with little artillery support until late afternoon.
The position fell when both flanks gave way after 14:00 and Ruggles massed about 53 guns against it (62 by the traditional count) while infantry closed in from three sides.
About 2,200 Union soldiers, Prentiss among them, were captured at 17:30, but the stand bought time for Webster's gun line above Pittsburg Landing.
The legend owes much to Prentiss's reports and to the park historian D. W. Reed, a 12th Iowa veteran; the NPS now notes that the deadliest fighting was on the flanks.

scenario.historyNote: The Sunken Road line held against about eight uncoordinated attacks from 10:30 to 15:30, then collapsed when its flanks gave way and Ruggles's massed guns opened, and about 2,200 Union soldiers including Prentiss surrendered at 17:30.

outcome: The Union line along the Sunken Road held for about seven hours against eight uncoordinated attacks (10:30-15:30 by the Staff Ride Handbook). It collapsed about 17:00-17:30, after the Union left fell back between about 14:00 and 16:00 and Sweeny's brigade on the right broke about 16:30 under massed Confederate guns (53 by the Staff Ride and Daniel, 62 by Ruggles, Reed and the older NPS handbook: Disputed).

About 2,200-2,300 Federals, Prentiss among them, were surrounded and captured, and W. H. L. Wallace was mortally wounded. The stand bought time: by about 17:00 Webster had about 52 guns on Grant's last line near Pittsburg Landing.
The NPS now argues that the Hornets' Nest was less central than the postwar tradition made it, and that the deadliest fighting at Shiloh was on the flanks.

casualties.basis: No source read gives losses for the Hornets' Nest fight alone. About 2,200 (or 2,300) Union soldiers were captured about 17:30 (Staff Ride; Daniel). Over the whole battle W. H. L. Wallace's 2nd Division lost 2,749 killed, wounded and missing (NPS plaque E); Gibson's Confederate brigade lost more than a quarter of its men in its four attacks (Staff Ride p.104).

scenario.title: Grant's last line
scenario.subtitle: The ridge above Pittsburg Landing and the Dill Branch ravine

victory.attackerHolds: The Confederates hold the ridge above Pittsburg Landing at 19:00. (In 1862 the attack across Dill Branch was thrown back.)
victory.defenderHolds: Grant's last line holds at 19:00, as it did in 1862.
victory.attackerBroken: The attack across Dill Branch has broken, as it did in 1862.
victory.draw: The ridge above the landing is still contested at 19:00.

text: By 17:30 the Sunken Road line has collapsed, but since 14:30 Grant's chief of staff, Col. Joseph D. Webster, has massed about 50 guns on the ridge above Pittsburg Landing, anchored by Madison's five 24-pounder siege guns.

Chalmers's and J. K. Jackson's brigades must cross the deep Dill Branch ravine under that fire while the gunboats Tyler and Lexington shell them from the river (their fire is not modelled here); Jackson's men have no ammunition and attack with the bayonet.
About 600 men of Nelson's division of Buell's army are across the river and in line by 18:00, so the stand is made mostly by Grant's own battered army.

The claim that one more hour of daylight would have won the battle for the Confederates is counterfactual: it ignores the ravine, the gun line, and the exhaustion and disorder their own officers described.

quote.text: Here the enemy made a last desperate effort to turn our flank, but was repelled.

scenario.positionsNote: The gun line follows the NPS tablets and monuments (Madison's battery monument, Markgraf's tablet coordinates) and the Handbook (Stand 15); Silversparre's exact spot is not sourced and is placed between them. Hurlbut stands on the right of the guns (Grant's Memoirs) and McClernand in the centre of the line further west (Daniel). The gunboats Tyler and Lexington and the routed remnant of W. H. L. Wallace's division are not fielded (see each phase note). All positions Inferred.
scenario.strengthNote: No formation has a sourced 18:00 strength. Hurlbut and McClernand are start-of-day present minus the day's killed, wounded and missing (a ceiling: stragglers are not removed); Chalmers is his own report's 2,039 less his losses; Jackson is a regiment-count share of Withers's division less his losses. Batteries carry a game crew of 20 per gun. Deas's and Anderson's brigades formed but did not attack (Handbook) and are left out.
scenario.historyNote: Chalmers's and Jackson's attack across Dill Branch about 18:00 was thrown back by Webster's gun line, the gunboats and the first of Buell's men, and Beauregard halted the army for the night.

outcome: The Confederate attack across Dill Branch failed. Jackson's brigade got no farther than the north slope of the ravine, Chalmers's repeated charges up the steep hill did not break the line, and Gage's battery was silenced, while Webster's guns and the gunboats Tyler and Lexington fired into the ravine.

Beauregard's order to stop for the night followed, with his men exhausted and disorganized. Ammen's brigade was across the river by about 19:30, Lew Wallace reached the right flank about 19:15 and Crittenden's division began arriving about 21:00. The gunboats shelled through the night, and Grant attacked at daylight on 7 April.

casualties.basis: No source gives losses for 17:30-19:00 alone. Whole-day losses: Chalmers's brigade 83 killed, 343 wounded and 19 missing, Jackson's 86, 364 and 194 (Staff Ride Handbook App. B); Ammen's brigade 16, 106 and 8 over both days. Markgraf's battery lost 3 wounded (NPS monument M116).

text: On 7 April Buell's Army of the Ohio and Grant's army attacked together: Nelson's, Crittenden's and McCook's divisions advanced from Pittsburg Landing while Lew Wallace's division attacked on the right.
Beauregard, who had telegraphed Richmond claiming a complete victory and did not know Buell had arrived, could count perhaps 20,000 effectives on the morning line (NPS).
Expect the hardest fighting in the Davis Wheat Field, Duncan Field and Woolf Field; Hazen's brigade took the heaviest Army of the Ohio losses.
This was a war to keep nearly four million people enslaved; neither the Confederates' early success nor Johnston's death changes what their army was fighting for.

scenario.positionsNote: Nelson's brigades (Ammen, Bruce, Hazen, left to right) start south of Dill Branch on the Hamburg-Savannah road, Crittenden's (Smith in front, Boyle behind) and McCook's (Rousseau, Kirk behind) to their right, and Lew Wallace's division north of Water Oaks Pond (Epperson, the 77th Pennsylvania history, Daniel). Wicker, Jones, Woolf and the Davis wheat field have no sourced coordinates, so the Confederate positions are placed by the fields that are mapped. All positions Inferred.
scenario.strengthNote: Army of the Ohio brigades are splits of the NPS plaque division totals (Nelson 4,541; Crittenden 3,825; McCook 7,552), not returns. Confederate 7 April strengths are Estimated: an average regiment of 408 (from Chalmers's report and Cleburne's compile figure) times regiments, less the brigade's two-day losses. Lew Wallace's 5,837 is the NPS plaque figure for the whole division.
scenario.historyNote: Nelson and Crittenden reached the Hamburg-Purdy road about 14:00 while McCook and Lew Wallace drove west toward Shiloh Church, and Beauregard withdrew to Corinth behind Breckinridge's rear guard.

outcome: Union victory. Attacking together on 7 April, Buell's Army of the Ohio and Grant's army drove the Confederates south through the camps they had lost the day before. Nelson and Crittenden reached the Hamburg-Purdy road about 14:00, while McCook pressed west through Woolf Field toward Water Oaks Pond and Shiloh Church.

Beauregard ordered a withdrawal to Corinth (the hour of the decision is Disputed, 13:00 to about 15:00), and Breckinridge's rear guard covered the retreat until about 17:00. Neither army pursued that night: exhaustion and Halleck's standing orders held Grant and Buell back, and on 8 April the retreating army was only probed.

casualties.basis: Whole-battle losses for both days: Union 13,047, Confederate 10,699 (Wikipedia and the American Battlefield Trust agree). No sourced figure splits the two days, so there is none for 7 April alone.
